title: What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples
web_title: 2. What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples
book_title: Chapter 2: What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples
question: What does PROV actually sell, to whom, and how much of the money comes from each part?

epigraph.quote: “Each kg of these products turns into more pouches than a kg of almonds or cashews.”
epigraph.author: Proventus Agrocom shareholders’ letter, 13 November 2026

web_blocks.html: Proventus reports a single business segment [1][3]. Every split in this chapter is therefore management’s own cut or our arithmetic on it, and we label each number as disclosed, derived or illustrative. Management cuts sales two ways: ProV brand against white-label and bulk, and core dry fruits against wholesome nutrition. Profit by segment is not disclosed anywhere. The only profit split that exists is by legal entity, and that is where this chapter ends.

Brand revenue is ₹659 crore of FY2026 consolidated revenue of ₹925.0 crore. White-label and bulk is the remainder, about ₹266 crore by our subtraction, and ₹177 crore (28%) in H1 FY27 by the company’s own figure [3][2]. Group sales are mostly one chain of goods, and the split depends on who the final buyer is.

web_blocks.caption: Revenue mix over time; ₹ crore, consolidated
web_blocks.takeaway: Sources: prospectus [10]; annual reports [15][3]; FY2026 presentation and H1 FY27 letter [5][2]. Derived columns are consolidated revenue less brand revenue; the FY2024 deck shows ₹170 crore for FY2024 against our ₹193 crore.

web_blocks.html: Two facts stand out. First, bulk and white-label did not disappear: it fell from ₹861 crore in FY2020 to about ₹165 crore in FY2025, then grew about 60% in FY2026. Second, the brand share has stopped rising. It was 71.7% in FY2025, 71.2% in FY2026 and 72.0% in H1 FY27. Brand revenue grew 61% in H1 FY27, and our estimate from the half-year figures is that bulk grew about 65%, so both lines are growing at the same pace [2]. The mix shift that drove the first three years of the story is paused, and the next stage depends on product mix inside the brand.

The brand sells packed dry fruits and snacks to households through four channels. Management splits brand sales into core dry fruits (almonds and cashews) and wholesome nutrition, which covers walnuts, pistachios, figs, dates, makhana, seeds, trail mixes, bars and nut chocolate. The annual report says core dry fruits were 52% of revenue in FY2026, down from 59% in FY2025, and wholesome nutrition 48%, up from 41% [3]. The report does not say whether ‘revenue’ here means brand revenue or total revenue, but the split sits beside the brand gross margin series.

web_blocks.html: The ladder shows why management pushes up the wholesome end: it expects its brand gross margin to rise with that share. The H1 FY27 letter reports 57% for ‘premium dry fruits and wholesome nutrition’ and calls the FY2025 figure 48%, which conflicts with the annual report’s 41% for FY2025 and 48% for FY2026 [2][3]. The wider label suggests a changed definition, so the 57% is not comparable with 48%. Volumes are clearer. Makhana, seeds, figs, dates and similar products grew from 440 tonnes in H1 FY26 to 1,700 tonnes in H1 FY27, about 27% of the 6,363 tonnes sold if that total covers the group [2]. Brand revenue of ₹456 crore on 2.07 crore pouches averages about ₹220 a pouch at invoice, which is our arithmetic and sits well above the ₹30 Minis.

An end-to-end example makes the chain concrete. We build it from disclosed mechanics, and the price is the only step not given. California packers, where the prospectus says the company had 30+ direct relationships, ship almonds to Mumbai. Proventus Agrocom, the listed parent, buys them: its foreign-currency import purchases were ₹281.4 crore in FY2026, 53% of its ₹530.2 crore of stock-in-trade purchases [3][10]. The parent then sells to its subsidiary Prov Foods at arm’s length. Sales to the subsidiary were ₹324.67 crore [3]. At the Khairane plant in Navi Mumbai, Prov Foods deshells, flavours and packs into pouches, with capacity of 1.5 lakh pouches a day [3]. A distributor supplies a kirana store, or the pack goes to a quick-commerce warehouse for Blinkit or Zepto. The MRP of a 500 g pack is not disclosed, and we have not invented one.

web_blocks.takeaway: Sources: prospectus [10]; FY2024 deck [17]; annual report FY2026 [3][5]; letter [2]. The FY2024 deck’s pie labels are jumbled in text, so channel years carry moderate confidence.

web_blocks.html: The brand has moved from a southern, general-trade and online product to a national, mixed-channel one. South India fell from about 71% to 41%, and the West now carries 37%. Because general trade, modern trade and e-commerce each carry meaningfully different terms, the shift matters for margin and receivables, and channel shares for FY2026 and H1 FY27 are not disclosed. In the prospectus (nine months to December 2022), top-five customers were 38% and top ten 51% of sales, and four of the top five were e-commerce or modern-trade names [10]. No later concentration figure exists.

This is the original business. The company sells bulk produce, processed and unprocessed, through the Navi Mumbai wholesale market and broker networks, and packs processed nuts for retail chains under their own labels. The website claims capacity to pack 1,00,000 packages a day for institutional buyers [10][38]. Revenue is about ₹266 crore in FY2026 by derivation and ₹177 crore in H1 FY27. Management gives three reasons for keeping it: market visibility, procurement scale and plant use [2]. No margin is disclosed, and no named customer.

The best evidence on its economics is the parent’s own result. The standalone company earned an EBITDA before other income of about 0.66% of its ₹535.3 crore revenue, roughly 66 paise on every ₹100 [3]. In our illustration, a mandi trader who buys a tonne of almonds from the parent pays import cost plus a spread of that order, and the price follows the commodity. The business offers volume and sourcing power and almost no margin. Management is candid that brand growth is the priority and bulk supports it [2].

web_blocks.title: Makhana and backward integration in Bihar

web_blocks.html: Makhana (fox nut) is the brand’s newest growth category. Bihar grows 80–90% of India’s supply, according to the government’s factsheet [51]. Prov Foods runs a unit at Billori in Purnia that the company says has 2,500 tonnes a year of capacity and began on 12 May 2026 [8]. The annual report calls Phase 1 operational [3]. A July 2026 press release says Bihar is being ‘progressively expanded’ towards 2,500 tonnes over three years, so we cannot tell whether the full figure is running today [7]. The company also claims the plant will add more than 300 bps of margin once running [5]. No revenue or margin for makhana is disclosed.

The annual report describes the route from pond to pack. Local farmers hand-harvest the seeds from ponds. They are sun-dried, roasted twice at up to 300°C, hand-popped, graded, seasoned and packed, then sold through the four channels [3]. The pack price is not disclosed. Annualising the 1,700-tonne half gives about 3,400 tonnes a year for the newer categories, so a full 2,500-tonne plant would equal roughly three-quarters of that. That group also includes figs, dates and seeds, so Bihar covers part of the supply, not all of it. This is our arithmetic, and the plant’s tonnes may be input weight.

Three smaller entities complete the group, and none changes the revenue picture. Proventus Commodities DMCC in Dubai sells bulk dry fruit and showed a ₹0.18 crore loss in FY2026 on turnover of about ₹3 crore as printed [10][3]. Proventus Retail sells ProV products to selected customers but had no turnover in FY2026 [10][3]. Pro-Nova Bio, 51% owned, turns shells and skins into bio-fuel briquettes for boilers. It made ₹0.73 crore of revenue in FY2022 and paused when the plant moved, and shows a ₹1.75 lakh loss in FY2026 [10][3]. All three together are below 1% of group revenue.

The listed parent’s own accounts mislead. Standalone revenue is ₹535.3 crore, but ₹324.67 crore of that is sold to Prov Foods, which is 61% [3]. Adding the two companies’ revenue would count the same nuts twice. The parent has 18 on-roll employees outside key management, so it works as a purchasing and financing company [3]. The table follows goods and money through the group.

web_blocks.html: The entity profit split is the only profit-by-business evidence we have. Prov Foods earned about 71% of consolidated PAT and the parent about 30%, offset by small losses elsewhere. Prov Foods’ own margin is 1.4% of turnover [3]. Another check: management’s 22.1% brand gross margin on ₹659 crore is ₹145.6 crore, while consolidated gross profit from the audited lines (revenue less materials, purchases and stock change) is ₹91.6 crore [3]. If both were measured the same way, bulk would have lost about ₹54 crore on ₹266 crore of sales, which is not credible. The definitions must differ, and a later chapter covers it. This means brand profitability cannot be checked from the filings.

web_blocks.the_number: About 79% of FY2026 white-label and bulk revenue, roughly ₹210 crore of ₹266 crore, is booked in the listed parent, not in Prov Foods.
web_blocks.how_calculated: The parent’s outside sales are ₹535.3 crore less ₹324.67 crore sold to Prov Foods, which is ₹210.6 crore. If all ₹659 crore of brand revenue sits in Prov Foods, that company’s outside non-brand sales are its turnover of ₹721.3 crore less ₹9.85 crore sold to the parent less ₹659 crore, or ₹52.5 crore. Adding the Dubai entity’s ₹3 crore gives ₹266.2 crore, which matches consolidated revenue less brand. The parent’s share is 210.6 divided by 266.2.
web_blocks.the_inputs: Standalone revenue and related-party sales [3]. Prov Foods turnover ₹721.3 crore (AOC-1) [3]. Brand revenue ₹659 crore [3][5]. Proventus Retail reports nil turnover, which supports the assumption that brand sales sit in Prov Foods [3].
web_blocks.the_range: 65% to 79%. If some ‘brand’ revenue is really institutional (see chapter 1), Prov Foods’ outside non-brand sales rise and the parent’s share falls. A brand revenue of ₹600 crore gives about 65%.
web_blocks.if_off: If the parent’s share is nearer 65%, more of the trading-type revenue sits in the manufacturing subsidiary and the brand entity is less pure than the headline suggests. If it is 79% or above, the parent is essentially a sourcing and trading arm that also lends ₹14.9 crore to its subsidiary.

web_blocks.html: The evidence shows a business that earns about 70% of its sales from a consumer brand, has stopped gaining share against bulk, makes goods through one subsidiary and sources through the parent. It does not show brand-level profit, makhana revenue, post-FY23 customer concentration or channel mix. Those gaps, rather than the headline growth, limit how far the filings can verify the brand story.

book_paragraphs: Let me walk you through what this company actually sells, because the headline hides the machinery. Imagine a 500-gram pack of almonds. You pick it off a kirana shelf in Bengaluru or tap it on a quick-commerce app. It says ProV. What happened before it got to you?

It starts in California. The prospectus says the company deals directly with more than thirty packers there. The almonds are shipped to Mumbai and bought by the listed parent, Proventus Agrocom. In FY2026 that parent spent ₹281 crore on imports. That is more than half of everything it purchased. The parent has only eighteen regular employees outside its senior managers. It does not make anything. It buys, holds stock and lends money to its subsidiary.

The parent then sells the nuts to Prov Foods, the subsidiary, at what the filings call arm’s length. Last year that was ₹325 crore, 61% of the parent’s own sales. Prov Foods runs the plant at Khairane. There the almonds are deshelled, flavoured, weighed and sealed into pouches, up to 1.5 lakh a day. A distributor takes the cartons to a kirana, or a quick-commerce warehouse takes them for Blinkit or Zepto. What does the pack cost you? The company does not tell us. The only price it discloses is ₹30 for a small ProV Minis pack, and I will not invent another.

Why do I make you follow the chain? Because it tells you not to add the parent’s ₹535 crore and the subsidiary’s ₹721 crore together. The ₹325 crore moves between them and gets counted twice. Strip it out, add the Dubai entity’s few crores, and you land at ₹925 crore of group revenue, almost to the rupee. When a company’s numbers reconcile like that, I relax a little. When its definitions do not, I do not, and we will come to that.

Now, what is ₹925 crore made of? Management says ₹659 crore is the ProV brand, which is 71%. The rest, about ₹266 crore, is white-label and bulk. That is the original trade: selling almonds by the tonne to mandi traders, and packing nuts for retail chains under someone else’s label. Nobody tells us its margin. But the parent’s own accounts keep 66 paise of EBITDA on every ₹100 of sales. Do you see why a business that is mostly the parent looks so thin? Bulk is a volume game with a commodity price on top.

Here is what surprised me. You would assume the brand keeps eating the bulk business. It has not. The brand share was 71.7% in FY2025, 71.2% in FY2026 and 72.0% in the first half of this year. Bulk grew right alongside it, by my estimate about 65% in the half-year against 61% for the brand. The company says it keeps bulk because it gives “close, continuous visibility into the dry-fruit and makhana markets”. That is a sensible reason. It also means the group is not becoming a pure brand business any time soon.

The brand itself is changing. Almonds and cashews were 59% of revenue in FY2025 and 52% in FY2026. Walnuts, pistachios, figs, dates, makhana, seeds and trail mixes took the rest. In the first half of this year those newer products grew from 440 tonnes to 1,700 tonnes. The CEO calls makhana “a generational category opportunity”. There is a neat piece of arithmetic behind the pouch count, and the November letter explains it: each kilo of seeds or makhana “turns into more pouches than a kg of almonds or cashews”. So pouch counts doubled while brand revenue grew 61%. Notice that this is a mix story, not only a volume story.

Now follow the pack outward. In FY2022 about seven of every ten rupees of brand sales came from five southern states: Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Telangana and Andhra Pradesh. By FY2026 the South was 41%, the West 37%, the North 16% and the East 6%. The channels moved too. In the FY2024 deck, general trade fell from about three-quarters of brand sales to a third, while modern trade and e-commerce rose to a third each. Quick commerce is now 5% to 7% of revenue, and management wants at least 10%. Why should you care? Because a kirana distributor, a hypermarket chain and an app all pay on different terms. Receivables at the end of September were ₹78.6 crore, double the March balance. A wider map brings more sales, and it also brings more people who have not yet paid you.

Picture Purnia in Bihar, where roughly four-fifths of India’s makhana grows. Farmers wade into shallow ponds and harvest the seeds by hand. The seeds are sun-dried, roasted twice at up to 300 degrees, hand-popped, graded and flavoured, then packed and sold. The company opened a plant there in May 2026 and calls its capacity 2,500 tonnes a year. A press release two months later says the plant is being expanded towards that figure over three years. I cannot tell you which statement describes today. I can tell you no revenue figure for makhana has been given.

Then there is the factory question. The Mumbai plant can pack 1.5 lakh pouches a day, and in the first half the company sold about 1.1 lakh a day. A new plant near Surat is planned to take capacity to more than 5 lakh. Why build so far ahead? The November letter answers plainly: “We are building Surat to support the scale we see the business achieving over the next two to three years, rather than just catering to current volumes.” That is an honest answer and also a bet. A plant is a promise about next year’s sales, paid for with this year’s cash.

A word on the smaller entities. A Dubai company sells bulk dry fruit and lost a little. A retail subsidiary had no sales. A 51% subsidiary that turned shells and skins into boiler fuel paused when the plant moved, and it is effectively dormant. Together they are under one percent of revenue. Do not spend your attention there.

Spend it on the one thing the filings will not give you: profit by business. The company reports a single segment. The only profit split is by legal entity, and it says Prov Foods earned about 71% of group profit and the parent about 30%. Management quotes a 22.1% brand gross margin, which on ₹659 crore would be ₹146 crore. The audited statements show total gross profit of ₹92 crore for the whole group. Both cannot be measured the same way. I do not say anyone is hiding anything. I say you cannot check the brand’s profit from the filings.

Here is my own judgment. About 79% of the white-label and bulk revenue, by my reading of the entity accounts, sits in the parent, and the brand sits in the subsidiary. The range is wide, 65% to 79%, because the definition of brand revenue is soft. So when you hear that this is a seventy-percent brand company, treat that as a good first approximation, not a measured fact.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: The business has two layers: a brand layer with a stated 22% gross margin that nobody outside can verify, and a trading layer that earns pennies and funds the volume. The honest question for the rest of this dossier is whether the first layer is large enough to carry the second.
